topic: Time passes faster at your head than at your feet
subject: science

sources.title: Measuring gravitational time dilation with delocalized quantum superpositions
Gravitational time dilation in extended quantum systems: The case of light clocks in Schwarzschild spacetime
Quantum time dilation in a gravitational field
A lab-based test of the gravitational redshift with a miniature clock network

facts.claim: The emission rate of an atom in a coherent superposition of separated wave packets in a gravitational field is different from the emission rate of an atom in a classical mixture of these packets.
facts.quote: In particular, we show that the emission rate of an atom prepared in a coherent superposition of separated wave packets in a gravitational field is different from the emission rate of an atom in a classical mixture of these packets, which gives rise to a quantum gravitational time dilation effect.

facts.claim: The time measured by a vertical light clock is equivalent to the proper time defined at its center.
facts.quote: In particular, we show that the time measured by the vertical light clock is equivalent to the proper time defined at its center.

facts.claim: Researchers measured a fractional frequency gradient of [ − 12.4 ± 0. 7 (stat) ± 2. 5 (sys) ] × 10 −19 /cm across a height difference of 1 cm.
facts.quote: We measure a fractional frequency gradient of [ − 12.4 ± 0. 7 (stat) ± 2. 5 (sys) ] × 10 −19 /cm, consistent with the expected redshift gradient of − 10.9 × 10 −19 /cm.

facts.claim: Time dilation was observed from relative speeds of less than 10 meters per second by comparing two optical atomic clocks connected by a 75-meter length of optical fiber.
facts.quote: We observed time dilation from relative speeds of less than 10 meters per second by comparing two optical atomic clocks connected by a 75-meter length of optical fiber.

facts.claim: Time dilation due to a change in height near Earth's surface of less than 1 meter can be detected.
facts.quote: We can now also detect time dilation due to a change in height near Earth's surface of less than 1 meter.
facts.causalWarning: causal wording, but the cited study only shows an association

facts.claim: A clock at a higher gravitational potential will tick faster than an otherwise identical clock at a lower potential.
facts.quote: Einstein’s theory of general relativity predicts that a clock at a higher gravitational potential will tick faster than an otherwise identical clock at a lower potential, an effect known as the gravitational redshift.

research.angle: Atomic clocks can detect gravitational time dilation over height differences of less than 1 meter, and quantum effects can create a nonclassical contribution to this dilation.
research.verdict: The evidence confirms that clocks at higher gravitational potentials tick faster, with measurements capable of detecting these differences at the centimeter and millimeter scales.
research.caveat: While the effect is measurable, the precision of these clocks is now reaching a regime where the physical size of the clock itself must be accounted for in the description.
